summary: Theo Chu, Anthropic PM for MCP, traces the protocol's origins to co-creators David and Justin, who noticed the friction of manually copying context from tools like Slack and Sentry into LLM context windows. Their insight was that models needed agency—the ability to reach into the real world and bring context and actions back. They concluded this required an open-source standardized protocol to avoid the BD and partnership overhead of closed ecosystems. MCP launched internally at an Anthropic hack week in November, went viral among engineers automating workflows, and was open-sourced shortly after. Initial external reception was skeptical, with questions about why a new protocol was needed when models could already call tools. Adoption took off when Cursor adopted MCP, followed by VS Code, Sourcegraph, and other coding tools, and more recently Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. Core design principles center on agents as the future, betting that model intelligence will scale and enable models to choose actions autonomously. The team believes there will be far more servers than clients, so they optimize for server simplicity, pushing complexity to clients. Recent updates include remote MCP support, a community-driven OAuth fix, streamable HTTP replacing SSE as the primary transport, and SDK and inspector tooling improvements. Future work includes elicitation, a registry API for model-discoverable MCPs, open-source example patterns, and long-term open governance. Theo frames agents as servers acting as clients and vice versa, enabling inter-agent communication. For startup opportunities, Theo emphasizes the ecosystem is still early and urges founders to build servers, allocating 80% of opportunity weight to building more servers, 10% to simplifying server building, and 10% to automated MCP generation. She stresses that high-quality servers must consider three users—the end user, the client developer, and the model—and should not simply wrap API endpoints one-to-one. She calls for servers beyond dev tools into verticals like sales, finance, legal, and education, and for tooling around hosting, testing, eval, and deployment. She identifies automated MCP server generation as a moonshot bet that models will eventually write their own MCPs in real time, and calls for AI security, observability, and auditing tooling as applications gain access to real-world data.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Theo introduces herself as an Anthropic PM working on MCP, former startup founder, with personal interests in poker and coffee.

sections.title: MCP Origin Story
sections.summary: Co-creators David and Justin observed constant copy-pasting of context from tools like Slack and Sentry into LLM context windows. The genesis was about model agency—letting models reach into the real world. They concluded it needed to be an open-source standardized protocol to work at scale.

sections.title: Launch and Adoption Trajectory
sections.summary: MCP launched at an Anthropic hack week in November, went viral internally, then was open-sourced. External reception was initially skeptical. Momentum came when Cursor adopted MCP, followed by VS Code, Sourcegraph, and recently Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI.

sections.title: Design Principles: Agents and Server Simplicity
sections.summary: Agents are the future direction; the protocol depends on model intelligence scaling. Streamable HTTP was adopted for bidirectionality. The team bets there will be more servers than clients, so they optimize for server simplicity, pushing complexity to clients.

sections.title: Recent Project Updates
sections.summary: Last six months: launched remote MCPs, fixed OAuth via community effort, adopted streamable HTTP as primary transport, updated SDKs and the Inspector debugging tool.

sections.title: Future Roadmap
sections.summary: Elicitation added to draft spec allows servers to ask users clarifying questions. Registry API in progress for model-discoverable MCPs. Developer experience improvements with open-source examples. Commitment to keeping MCP open forever with governance updates coming.

sections.title: Agents Architecture and Transition to Startup Opportunities
sections.summary: Theo describes agents as servers acting as clients and vice versa, enabling inter-agent communication. Transitions to the anticipated section on what founders should build in the MCP ecosystem.

sections.title: Startup Opportunities: Build More Servers
sections.summary: Theo emphasizes the ecosystem is still early and urges founders to build more servers. She allocates 80% of opportunity weight to building servers, 10% to simplifying server building, and 10% to automated MCP generation.

sections.title: Higher Quality Servers and New Verticals
sections.summary: Theo argues against simply wrapping API endpoints one-to-one as MCP tools. High-quality servers must consider three users: the end user, the client developer, and the model. She calls for servers beyond dev tools into verticals like sales, finance, legal, and education.

sections.title: Simplifying Server Building
sections.summary: Given the belief that servers will vastly outnumber clients, Theo calls for tooling to make server building easier—hosting, testing, eval, deployment—for enterprises deploying internal MCPs and indie hackers building for external users.

sections.title: Automated MCP Generation, Security, and Closing
sections.summary: Theo identifies automated MCP server generation as a moonshot bet that models will eventually write their own MCPs in real time. She also calls for AI security, observability, and auditing tooling as applications gain access to real-world data. Closes with 'happy MCP.'

demonstrations: Elicitation example: a flight booking server asks the end user what 'best flight' means—cheapest or fastest—then passes the response back
